rationale: B wins narrowly because it gives the founder a sharper newsroom map: “retail-operations reporter at an apparel or retail trade outlet covering store-level service models and reverse logistics” is a real desk, not a misty sustainability bucket. A is disciplined, but it splits one tension into two angles: “500,000 used items” and “won’t say how much money its sustainability story makes” are cousins in different jackets. B still needs a leash on “nobody else can copy the math”; without cost data, that line is too cocky by half.
gaps_in_A: “Patagonia opens free repairs at every US store” overstates the offer. The facts say basic repairs are free and complex repairs are charged at cost; the headline makes free sound broader than it is.

“A sustainable-fashion or circular-economy trade reporter” is competent but a little bucket-y. The stronger first lens is retail operations, repair logistics, or right-to-repair with an actual outside peg.

The data and contrarian angles lean on the same missing denominator: “500,000 resold items” plus “will not say what share of revenue resale represents.” That may be one better angle, not two clean pitches.

“Next step: newsjack-detector” is not the cleanest next move. The announcement itself is the peg; the more urgent question is whether this rollout is materially new versus already-covered Worn Wear history.
gaps_in_B: “A company with no shareholders” is not supported by “privately held.” Patagonia’s ownership is unusual, but the update does not give you license to flatten the corporate structure into a bumper sticker.
“nobody else can copy the math” is an unproven economics claim. The set admits it needs cost data, then lets the headline sprint ahead of the evidence anyway.
“category-creation” is inflated. A nationwide repair expansion may be a category signal, but the update does not prove Patagonia created a category.

“the publicly traded peer who can’t do this” invents a competitor constraint. The update gives no peer economics, no repair cost, and no evidence that public apparel companies cannot run similar programs.
